q: What does EBS stand for in AWS?

exp.a: Correct. EBS stands for Elastic Block Store, a block-level storage service for EC2 instances.
exp.b: Incorrect. There is no AWS service called Elastic Byte Storage.
exp.c: Incorrect. Extended Block Store is not a valid AWS term.
exp.d: Incorrect. Elastic Backup Service is not what EBS stands for; AWS Backup is a separate service.

q: What type of storage does Amazon EBS provide?

exp.a: Incorrect. Object storage is provided by Amazon S3.
exp.b: Correct. EBS provides block-level storage volumes for use with EC2 instances.
exp.c: Incorrect. File storage is provided by Amazon EFS and FSx.
exp.d: Incorrect. Tape storage is not provided by EBS; AWS Storage Gateway offers virtual tape.

q: EBS volumes are bound to which scope?

exp.a: Incorrect. EBS volumes are not region-scoped; they exist within a specific Availability Zone.
exp.b: Correct. An EBS volume is created in a specific Availability Zone and can only be attached to instances in that same AZ.
exp.c: Incorrect. EBS volumes are not globally available.
exp.d: Incorrect. EBS volumes are not VPC-scoped; they are AZ-scoped.

q: Can an EBS volume be attached to multiple EC2 instances at the same time by default?

opts.b: No, only one instance at a time (unless using Multi-Attach)

exp.a: Incorrect. By default, a standard EBS volume can only be attached to one instance.
exp.b: Correct. By default, one EBS volume attaches to one EC2 instance, but io1/io2 volumes support Multi-Attach for up to 16 instances.
exp.c: Incorrect. There is no default limit of 5 instances for standard attachment.
exp.d: Incorrect. With Multi-Attach feature on io1/io2, multiple instances can attach to the same volume.

q: Which EBS volume types support the Multi-Attach feature?

exp.a: Incorrect. General Purpose SSD volumes (gp2/gp3) do not support Multi-Attach.
exp.b: Correct. Only Provisioned IOPS SSD volumes (io1 and io2) support the Multi-Attach feature.
exp.c: Incorrect. Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) and Cold HDD (sc1) do not support Multi-Attach.
exp.d: Incorrect. Multi-Attach is limited to io1/io2 volume types only.

q: What is the maximum number of instances that can be attached to a single EBS volume using Multi-Attach?

exp.a: Incorrect. The limit is not 4 instances.
exp.b: Incorrect. The limit is not 8 instances.
exp.c: Correct. Multi-Attach allows up to 16 EC2 instances to be attached to a single io1/io2 EBS volume simultaneously.
exp.d: Incorrect. The limit is 16, not 32.

q: What is the minimum volume size for an EBS gp2/gp3 volume?

exp.a: Correct. The minimum size for gp2 and gp3 volumes is 1 GiB.
exp.b: Incorrect. 4 GiB is not the minimum size for gp2/gp3.
exp.c: Incorrect. 8 GiB is not the minimum; it is 1 GiB.
exp.d: Incorrect. 10 GiB is not the minimum size.

q: What is the maximum volume size for an EBS gp2/gp3 volume?

exp.a: Incorrect. 1 TiB is not the maximum for gp2/gp3.
exp.b: Incorrect. 4 TiB is not the maximum for gp2/gp3.
exp.c: Correct. The maximum size for gp2 and gp3 volumes is 16 TiB.
exp.d: Incorrect. 64 TiB exceeds the maximum EBS volume size.

q: What is the maximum IOPS for a gp2 EBS volume?

exp.a: Incorrect. 3,000 IOPS is the baseline/burst for small gp2 volumes, not the maximum.
exp.b: Incorrect. 10,000 IOPS is not the maximum for gp2.
exp.c: Correct. gp2 volumes can deliver a maximum of 16,000 IOPS.
exp.d: Incorrect. 64,000 IOPS is the maximum for io1/io2 volumes, not gp2.

q: What is the maximum IOPS for a gp3 EBS volume?

exp.a: Incorrect. 3,000 IOPS is the baseline for gp3, not the maximum.
exp.b: Correct. gp3 volumes can be provisioned up to a maximum of 16,000 IOPS.
exp.c: Incorrect. 32,000 IOPS exceeds the gp3 maximum.
exp.d: Incorrect. 64,000 IOPS is the maximum for io1/io2, not gp3.

q: What is the baseline IOPS for a gp3 volume?

exp.a: Incorrect. The baseline is not 1,000 IOPS for gp3.
exp.b: Correct. gp3 volumes provide a baseline of 3,000 IOPS regardless of volume size.
exp.c: Incorrect. 5,000 IOPS is not the gp3 baseline.
exp.d: Incorrect. 10,000 IOPS is not the baseline for gp3.

q: What is the baseline throughput for a gp3 volume?

exp.a: Incorrect. 64 MiB/s is not the baseline throughput for gp3.
exp.b: Correct. gp3 volumes provide a baseline throughput of 125 MiB/s.
exp.c: Incorrect. 250 MiB/s is not the baseline; gp3 can be provisioned up to 1,000 MiB/s.
exp.d: Incorrect. 500 MiB/s is above the baseline for gp3.

q: What is the maximum throughput for a gp3 volume?

exp.a: Incorrect. 250 MiB/s is the maximum throughput for gp2, not gp3.
exp.b: Incorrect. 500 MiB/s is the maximum throughput for st1, not gp3.
exp.c: Correct. gp3 volumes can be provisioned up to 1,000 MiB/s throughput.
exp.d: Incorrect. 2,000 MiB/s exceeds the gp3 maximum throughput.

q: How does gp2 calculate its IOPS performance?

opts.b: 3 IOPS per GiB with a minimum burst of 3,000 IOPS

exp.a: Incorrect. IOPS scales with volume size in gp2, it is not always fixed at 3,000.
exp.b: Correct. gp2 provides 3 IOPS per GiB of volume size, with a burst capability of up to 3,000 IOPS for volumes under 1,000 GiB.
exp.c: Incorrect. 10 IOPS per GiB is not the gp2 formula.
exp.d: Incorrect. 50 IOPS per GiB applies to io1/io2 ratio, not gp2.

q: What is the maximum IOPS for an io1 EBS volume?

exp.a: Incorrect. 16,000 IOPS is the max for gp2/gp3.
exp.b: Incorrect. 32,000 IOPS is not the max for io1.
exp.c: Correct. io1 volumes support a maximum of 64,000 IOPS.
exp.d: Incorrect. 256,000 IOPS is the max for io2 Block Express, not standard io1.

q: What is the maximum IOPS for an io2 Block Express EBS volume?

exp.a: Incorrect. 64,000 IOPS is the max for standard io1/io2.
exp.b: Incorrect. 128,000 is not the correct maximum for io2 Block Express.
exp.c: Correct. io2 Block Express supports up to 256,000 IOPS.
exp.d: Incorrect. 500,000 IOPS exceeds the io2 Block Express maximum.

q: What is the IOPS-to-GiB ratio for io1 volumes?

exp.a: Incorrect. 3 IOPS per GiB applies to gp2 volumes.
exp.b: Incorrect. 10 IOPS per GiB is not the io1 ratio.
exp.c: Correct. io1 volumes support up to 50 IOPS per GiB of provisioned storage.
exp.d: Incorrect. 100 IOPS per GiB is not the correct ratio for io1.

q: What is the IOPS-to-GiB ratio for io2 Block Express volumes?

exp.a: Incorrect. 50 IOPS per GiB applies to io1.
exp.b: Incorrect. 100 IOPS per GiB is not the ratio for io2 Block Express.
exp.c: Incorrect. 500 IOPS per GiB is not the correct ratio.
exp.d: Correct. io2 Block Express supports up to 1,000 IOPS per GiB.

q: What is the maximum volume size for io2 Block Express?

exp.a: Incorrect. 16 TiB is the max for standard EBS volumes like gp2/gp3/io1.
exp.b: Incorrect. 32 TiB is not the max for io2 Block Express.
exp.c: Correct. io2 Block Express volumes can be up to 64 TiB in size.
exp.d: Incorrect. 128 TiB exceeds the maximum for io2 Block Express.

q: Which EBS volume type is best suited for boot volumes?

exp.a: Incorrect. st1 cannot be used as a boot volume.
exp.b: Incorrect. sc1 cannot be used as a boot volume.
exp.c: Correct. gp2 and gp3 (General Purpose SSD) are recommended for boot volumes due to their SSD performance.
exp.d: Incorrect. While magnetic can be a boot volume, gp2/gp3 are the recommended choices.

q: Which EBS volume types CANNOT be used as boot volumes?

exp.a: Incorrect. gp2 and gp3 can be used as boot volumes.
exp.b: Incorrect. io1 and io2 can be used as boot volumes.
exp.c: Correct. HDD-based volumes (st1 and sc1) cannot be used as boot volumes.
exp.d: Incorrect. Both gp3 and io2 can be used as boot volumes.

q: What is the maximum throughput for an st1 (Throughput Optimized HDD) volume?

exp.a: Incorrect. 250 MiB/s is the max throughput for sc1 and gp2.
exp.b: Correct. st1 volumes can achieve a maximum throughput of 500 MiB/s.
exp.c: Incorrect. 1,000 MiB/s is the max throughput for gp3.
exp.d: Incorrect. 125 MiB/s is the baseline throughput for gp3.

q: What is the maximum throughput for an sc1 (Cold HDD) volume?

exp.a: Incorrect. 125 MiB/s is not the max throughput for sc1.
exp.b: Correct. sc1 volumes can achieve a maximum throughput of 250 MiB/s.
exp.c: Incorrect. 500 MiB/s is the max throughput for st1.
exp.d: Incorrect. 40 MiB/s is too low for sc1 max throughput.

q: What is the maximum IOPS for an st1 volume?

exp.a: Incorrect. 250 IOPS is the max for sc1, not st1.
exp.b: Correct. st1 volumes support a maximum of 500 IOPS.
exp.c: Incorrect. 1,000 IOPS exceeds st1 capability.
exp.d: Incorrect. 16,000 IOPS is the max for gp2/gp3, not st1.

q: What is the maximum IOPS for an sc1 volume?

exp.a: Incorrect. 100 IOPS is not the max for sc1.
exp.b: Correct. sc1 volumes support a maximum of 250 IOPS.
exp.c: Incorrect. 500 IOPS is the max for st1, not sc1.
exp.d: Incorrect. 1,000 IOPS far exceeds sc1 capability.

q: What is the minimum size for st1 and sc1 volumes?

exp.a: Incorrect. 1 GiB is the minimum for gp2/gp3, not st1/sc1.
exp.b: Correct. Both st1 and sc1 volumes have a minimum size of 125 GiB.
exp.c: Incorrect. 500 GiB is not the minimum for st1/sc1.
exp.d: Incorrect. 1,000 GiB is not the minimum for these volume types.

q: What happens to an EBS volume when the attached EC2 instance is terminated, if 'Delete on Termination' is enabled?

opts.a: The volume is detached and remains available
opts.c: The volume is converted to a snapshot
opts.d: The volume is moved to another AZ

exp.a: Incorrect. With Delete on Termination enabled, the volume does not persist.
exp.b: Correct. When Delete on Termination is enabled, the EBS volume is deleted when the instance terminates.
exp.c: Incorrect. The volume is not automatically converted to a snapshot.
exp.d: Incorrect. The volume is not moved; it is deleted.

q: By default, is 'Delete on Termination' enabled for the root EBS volume?

exp.a: Correct. By default, the root EBS volume has Delete on Termination enabled.
exp.b: Incorrect. The root volume does have Delete on Termination enabled by default.
exp.c: Incorrect. It applies to all root volumes regardless of type.
exp.d: Incorrect. It applies to all root volumes regardless of type.

q: By default, is 'Delete on Termination' enabled for additional (non-root) EBS volumes?

opts.c: Only if the volume is encrypted

exp.a: Incorrect. Additional EBS volumes do NOT have Delete on Termination enabled by default.
exp.b: Correct. By default, additional (non-root) EBS volumes are NOT deleted when the instance terminates.
exp.c: Incorrect. Encryption status does not affect the default Delete on Termination setting.
exp.d: Incorrect. Volume type does not affect the default Delete on Termination setting for non-root volumes.

q: What is an EBS Snapshot?

opts.a: A real-time copy of the volume in another AZ
opts.b: A point-in-time backup of an EBS volume
opts.c: A compressed version of the volume
opts.d: A live mirror of the volume

exp.a: Incorrect. Snapshots are not real-time copies; they are point-in-time backups.
exp.b: Correct. An EBS snapshot is a point-in-time backup of an EBS volume stored in Amazon S3.
exp.c: Incorrect. While snapshots are incremental and space-efficient, they are backups, not compressed versions.
exp.d: Incorrect. Snapshots are not live mirrors.

q: Are EBS snapshots incremental?

opts.a: No, each snapshot is a full copy
opts.b: Yes, only changed blocks are stored in subsequent snapshots

exp.a: Incorrect. EBS snapshots are incremental, not full copies each time.
exp.b: Correct. EBS snapshots are incremental — only the blocks that have changed since the last snapshot are saved.
exp.c: Incorrect. Incremental snapshots apply to all EBS volume types.
exp.d: Incorrect. Incremental snapshots apply to all EBS volume types.

q: Can you create an EBS volume in a different Availability Zone from a snapshot?

opts.a: No, the volume must be in the same AZ as the snapshot
opts.b: Yes, you can restore a snapshot to any AZ within the same region
opts.c: Only if you use Cross-Region Replication

exp.a: Incorrect. Snapshots can be used to create volumes in any AZ within the region.
exp.b: Correct. You can create an EBS volume from a snapshot in any Availability Zone within the same region.
exp.c: Incorrect. Cross-Region Replication is for copying snapshots to another region, not for creating volumes in a different AZ.
exp.d: Incorrect. This capability applies to snapshots of all volume types.

q: Where are EBS snapshots stored?

exp.a: Incorrect. Snapshots are not stored in the EBS volume itself.
exp.b: Correct. EBS snapshots are stored in Amazon S3, managed by AWS (not visible in your S3 buckets).
exp.c: Incorrect. By default, snapshots are stored in S3, not Glacier. However, you can archive them to a snapshot archive tier.
exp.d: Incorrect. Instance store is ephemeral and not used for snapshot storage.

q: What is the EBS Snapshot Archive tier?

opts.a: A faster storage tier for frequently accessed snapshots
opts.b: A lower-cost storage tier that is 75% cheaper, with 24-72 hours restore time
opts.d: A tier that automatically deletes old snapshots

exp.a: Incorrect. The Archive tier is for infrequently accessed snapshots, not faster access.
exp.b: Correct. The EBS Snapshot Archive tier is 75% cheaper but takes 24-72 hours to restore.
exp.c: Incorrect. It is not a replication feature.
exp.d: Incorrect. It does not automatically delete snapshots.

q: What is the EBS Recycle Bin?

opts.a: A feature to compress unused EBS volumes
opts.b: A feature to recover accidentally deleted EBS snapshots
opts.c: A feature to automatically archive old volumes
opts.d: A feature to delete volumes after 30 days

exp.a: Incorrect. Recycle Bin does not compress volumes.
exp.b: Correct. The EBS Recycle Bin allows you to recover accidentally deleted EBS snapshots by retaining them for a specified period.
exp.c: Incorrect. Recycle Bin is specifically for deleted snapshot recovery.
exp.d: Incorrect. Recycle Bin retains deleted snapshots, not deletes volumes.

q: What retention period can you set for the EBS Recycle Bin?

exp.a: Correct. You can set a retention period from 1 day to 1 year (365 days) for the EBS Recycle Bin.
exp.b: Incorrect. 7 days is not the only option.
exp.c: Incorrect. 30 days is not the only option.
exp.d: Incorrect. There is a maximum retention of 1 year.

q: Can you copy an EBS snapshot to another AWS region?

opts.b: Yes, you can copy snapshots across regions

exp.a: Incorrect. Snapshots can be copied across regions.
exp.b: Correct. You can copy EBS snapshots to other AWS regions for disaster recovery or migration.
exp.c: Incorrect. Both encrypted and unencrypted snapshots can be copied across regions.
exp.d: Incorrect. Snapshots of all volume types can be copied across regions.

q: What encryption algorithm does EBS use for volume encryption?

exp.a: Incorrect. EBS does not use AES-128.
exp.b: Correct. EBS encryption uses AES-256 algorithm.
exp.c: Incorrect. RSA-2048 is an asymmetric encryption algorithm, not used for EBS volume encryption.
exp.d: Incorrect. SHA-256 is a hashing algorithm, not an encryption algorithm.

q: Which AWS service manages the encryption keys used by EBS encryption by default?

exp.a: Incorrect. IAM manages access permissions, not encryption keys for EBS.
exp.b: Correct. EBS encryption uses AWS KMS (Key Management Service) to manage encryption keys.
exp.c: Incorrect. CloudHSM can be used but is not the default key management service for EBS.
exp.d: Incorrect. Secrets Manager is for storing secrets, not for EBS encryption key management.

q: Does EBS encryption have a significant impact on latency?

opts.b: No, encryption and decryption are handled transparently with minimal impact

exp.a: Incorrect. EBS encryption does not double latency.
exp.b: Correct. EBS encryption/decryption is handled transparently by EC2 and EBS infrastructure with minimal latency impact.
exp.c: Incorrect. The latency impact is minimal, not 50%.
exp.d: Incorrect. Encryption impact is minimal for all volume types.

q: How can you encrypt an existing unencrypted EBS volume?

opts.a: Enable encryption directly on the volume
opts.b: Create a snapshot, copy the snapshot with encryption enabled, then create a new volume from the encrypted snapshot
opts.c: Use AWS CLI to toggle encryption

exp.a: Incorrect. You cannot enable encryption directly on an existing unencrypted volume.
exp.b: Correct. To encrypt an unencrypted volume: create a snapshot → copy snapshot with encryption → create new encrypted volume from the encrypted snapshot.
exp.c: Incorrect. There is no CLI command to toggle encryption on an existing volume.
exp.d: Incorrect. Detaching and re-attaching does not encrypt the volume.

q: When you create an encrypted EBS volume, what is also encrypted?

opts.b: Data at rest, data in transit between the volume and instance, all snapshots, and volumes created from snapshots

exp.a: Incorrect. Encryption covers more than just data at rest.
exp.b: Correct. EBS encryption encrypts data at rest, data in flight between EC2 and EBS, all snapshots created from the volume, and all volumes created from those snapshots.
exp.c: Incorrect. Both data and snapshots are encrypted.
exp.d: Incorrect. Data at rest is also encrypted.

q: What is an EC2 Instance Store?

opts.b: A physically attached high-performance ephemeral storage

exp.a: Incorrect. Network-attached storage describes EBS, not Instance Store.
exp.b: Correct. EC2 Instance Store is physically attached storage on the host providing very high I/O performance but is ephemeral (data is lost on stop/terminate).
exp.c: Incorrect. Managed file systems are EFS or FSx.
exp.d: Incorrect. Instance Store is not S3-backed.

q: What happens to data on an EC2 Instance Store when the instance is stopped or terminated?

opts.c: Data is automatically backed up to S3

exp.a: Incorrect. Instance Store data is NOT preserved on stop or termination.
exp.b: Correct. Instance Store is ephemeral — data is lost when the instance is stopped, terminated, or the underlying hardware fails.
exp.c: Incorrect. Data is not automatically backed up.
exp.d: Incorrect. Data is not automatically moved to EBS.

q: What is Amazon EFS?

opts.a: Elastic File System — a managed NFS file system
opts.c: Extended File Service — a tape backup system
opts.d: Encrypted File Store — an encryption service

exp.a: Correct. Amazon EFS (Elastic File System) is a managed NFS (Network File System) that can be mounted on multiple EC2 instances.
exp.b: Incorrect. EFS does not stand for Elastic Flash Storage.
exp.c: Incorrect. EFS is not a tape backup system.
exp.d: Incorrect. EFS is not an encryption service.

q: What is a key difference between EBS and EFS?

opts.a: EBS can be mounted on multiple instances across AZs; EFS cannot
opts.b: EFS can be mounted on multiple instances across AZs; EBS is AZ-specific
opts.c: EBS is a file system; EFS is block storage

exp.a: Incorrect. EBS is AZ-specific (unless using Multi-Attach for io1/io2 in the same AZ).
exp.b: Correct. EFS is a shared file system that can be mounted across multiple EC2 instances in multiple AZs, while EBS is locked to one AZ.
exp.c: Incorrect. EBS is block storage and EFS is a file system.
exp.d: Incorrect. There are significant differences between EBS and EFS.

q: Is EBS a network-attached storage?

opts.a: No, it is physically attached to the instance
opts.b: Yes, it communicates over the network to the EC2 instance

exp.a: Incorrect. Physical attachment describes Instance Store, not EBS.
exp.b: Correct. EBS is network-attached storage, meaning there may be slight latency as it communicates over the network.
exp.c: Incorrect. All EBS volume types are network-attached.
exp.d: Incorrect. EBS is network-attached in all regions.

q: Can you increase the size of an EBS volume without detaching it?

opts.a: No, you must detach the volume first
opts.b: Yes, you can use Elastic Volumes to modify size, type, and IOPS without detaching
opts.d: Only if the instance is stopped

exp.a: Incorrect. EBS Elastic Volumes allows modification without detaching.
exp.b: Correct. With Elastic Volumes, you can increase size, change volume type, and adjust IOPS/throughput while the volume is attached and in use.
exp.c: Incorrect. Elastic Volumes works with all volume types.
exp.d: Incorrect. The instance does not need to be stopped.

q: Can you decrease the size of an EBS volume?

opts.a: Yes, you can decrease the size at any time
opts.b: No, you can only increase the size of an EBS volume
opts.c: Yes, but only for gp3 volumes

exp.a: Incorrect. You cannot decrease the size of an EBS volume.
exp.b: Correct. EBS volumes can only be increased in size, never decreased. To get a smaller volume, you must create a new smaller volume and migrate data.
exp.c: Incorrect. No volume type supports size reduction.
exp.d: Incorrect. You cannot decrease volume size under any circumstance.

q: After increasing an EBS volume size, what additional step might be required?

opts.b: Extend the file system within the OS to use the additional space

exp.a: Incorrect. A reboot is not always required.
exp.b: Correct. After resizing an EBS volume, you must extend the file system within the operating system to utilize the new space.
exp.c: Incorrect. Creating a snapshot is not required after resizing.
exp.d: Incorrect. You do not need to detach and re-attach.

q: What is the durability of EBS volumes?

exp.a: Incorrect. This is incomplete.
exp.b: Correct. Standard EBS volumes (gp2/gp3/st1/sc1) offer 99.8%-99.9% durability, while io1/io2 offer 99.999% durability.
exp.c: Incorrect. Durability varies by volume type.
exp.d: Incorrect. No storage service guarantees 100% durability.

q: What is the SLA availability for EBS volumes?

exp.a: Incorrect. 99.0% is too low for EBS SLA.
exp.b: Incorrect. 99.9% is lower than the actual EBS SLA.
exp.c: Correct. EBS provides an SLA of 99.99% availability.
exp.d: Incorrect. 99.999% is the durability for io1/io2, not the availability SLA.

q: What is an EBS-optimized instance?

opts.a: An instance that uses only Instance Store
opts.b: An instance with dedicated bandwidth for EBS I/O, separate from network traffic
opts.c: An instance that can only use gp3 volumes
opts.d: An instance with no network connectivity

exp.a: Incorrect. EBS-optimized instances use EBS volumes, not just Instance Store.
exp.b: Correct. EBS-optimized instances provide dedicated throughput between EC2 and EBS, minimizing contention with other network traffic.
exp.c: Incorrect. EBS-optimized instances can use any EBS volume type.
exp.d: Incorrect. EBS-optimized instances still have network connectivity.

q: How many EBS volumes can you attach to a single EC2 instance (approximate maximum)?

exp.a: Incorrect. You can attach more than 5 volumes.
exp.b: Incorrect. The limit is higher than 10.
exp.c: Correct. You can typically attach up to 28 EBS volumes to a single EC2 instance (limit varies by instance type, with some Nitro instances supporting more).
exp.d: Incorrect. 128 is too high for standard instances.

q: What is Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM) used for with EBS?

opts.b: To automate the creation, retention, and deletion of EBS snapshots

exp.a: Incorrect. DLM does not resize volumes.
exp.b: Correct. Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager automates the creation, retention, and deletion of EBS snapshots based on policies.
exp.c: Incorrect. Performance monitoring is done by CloudWatch, not DLM.
exp.d: Incorrect. DLM does not handle encryption.

q: Which CloudWatch metric is used to monitor the percentage of I/O operations delivered for an EBS volume?

exp.a: Incorrect. VolumeReadOps counts read operations, not delivery percentage.
exp.b: Incorrect. VolumeQueueLength shows the number of pending I/O requests.
exp.c: Correct. VolumeThroughputPercentage indicates the percentage of IOPS delivered relative to provisioned IOPS (for io1/io2).
exp.d: Incorrect. BurstBalance shows remaining burst credits for gp2/st1/sc1.

q: What does the BurstBalance CloudWatch metric indicate for EBS volumes?

opts.b: The percentage of I/O burst credits remaining

exp.a: Incorrect. BurstBalance does not show current IOPS usage directly.
exp.b: Correct. BurstBalance shows the percentage of I/O burst credits remaining for gp2, st1, and sc1 volumes.
exp.c: Incorrect. Volume size is not represented by BurstBalance.
exp.d: Incorrect. Encryption status is not a CloudWatch metric.

q: Which EBS volume type is most cost-effective for infrequently accessed data that requires low-cost storage?

exp.a: Incorrect. gp3 is for general-purpose workloads, not the cheapest for cold data.
exp.b: Incorrect. io2 is the most expensive EBS option.
exp.c: Incorrect. st1 is for frequently accessed throughput-intensive workloads.
exp.d: Correct. sc1 (Cold HDD) is the lowest-cost EBS volume type, designed for infrequently accessed data.

q: Which EBS volume type would you choose for a Big Data or data warehouse workload requiring high throughput?

exp.a: Incorrect. gp2 is general purpose, not optimized for sequential throughput.
exp.b: Incorrect. io1 is for high IOPS workloads like databases, not throughput-heavy workloads.
exp.c: Correct. st1 (Throughput Optimized HDD) is ideal for Big Data, data warehouses, and log processing that require high sequential throughput.
exp.d: Incorrect. sc1 is for cold/infrequently accessed data with lower throughput.

q: Which EBS volume type is best for database workloads requiring sustained high IOPS?

exp.a: Incorrect. gp2 is suitable for moderate database workloads but not sustained very high IOPS.
exp.b: Correct. io1/io2 (Provisioned IOPS SSD) are designed for critical database workloads requiring sustained high IOPS performance.
exp.c: Incorrect. st1 is an HDD type not suited for database IOPS workloads.
exp.d: Incorrect. sc1 is for cold storage, not database workloads.

q: Can an EBS volume be attached to an EC2 instance in a different Availability Zone?

opts.b: No, the volume and instance must be in the same AZ

exp.a: Incorrect. You cannot directly attach an EBS volume to an instance in a different AZ.
exp.b: Correct. An EBS volume can only be attached to an EC2 instance in the same Availability Zone.
exp.c: Incorrect. Even io1/io2 volumes must be in the same AZ as the instance.
exp.d: Incorrect. VPC peering does not enable cross-AZ EBS attachment.

q: How can you move an EBS volume to another Availability Zone?

opts.a: Detach it and re-attach to the other AZ
opts.b: Create a snapshot of the volume and then create a new volume from the snapshot in the target AZ

exp.a: Incorrect. You cannot simply detach and attach across AZs.
exp.b: Correct. To move an EBS volume to another AZ, create a snapshot and then create a new volume from that snapshot in the desired AZ.
exp.c: Incorrect. Direct Connect is for network connectivity to AWS, not for moving EBS volumes.
exp.d: Incorrect. VPC endpoints are for accessing AWS services privately, not for moving volumes.

q: What is the default EBS volume type when creating an EC2 instance through the AWS Console?

q: What is Fast Snapshot Restore (FSR) in EBS?

opts.a: A feature that reduces snapshot creation time
opts.b: A feature that eliminates the latency of data loading when creating a volume from a snapshot

exp.c: Incorrect. FSR is not related to encryption speed.
exp.d: Incorrect. FSR does not compress snapshots.
